summary: This NBER working paper (No. 14596, December 2008) by Andreas Beyer, Vitor Gaspar, Christina Gerberding and Otmar Issing examines how the Bundesbank's monetary targeting strategy supported German price stability in the 1970s and 1980s. The authors frame monetary targeting as a commitment device that anchors inflation expectations, derive an interest rate rule, and show it approximates Bundesbank policy over 1975-1998. They find strong policy-rate persistence and a strong response to inflation and activity growth gaps, but no significant response to the output gap level, using real-time data.
one_line: NBER working paper analyzing how Bundesbank monetary targeting anchored German inflation expectations and shaped its policy rule from 1975 to 1998.
key_facts: NBER Working Paper 14596 was issued in December 2008 and carries DOI 10.3386/w14596.
The paper is authored by Andreas Beyer, Vitor Gaspar, Christina Gerberding and Otmar Issing.
The paper examines the Bundesbank's monetary policy strategy during the turbulent 1970s and 1980s.
The authors state that the Bundesbank established an outstanding reputation in central banking and provided the role model for the European Central Bank.
The paper proposes a theoretical framework, following Söderström (2005), in which monetary targeting is interpreted first and foremost as a commitment device.
The authors argue that a monetary target helps anchor inflation and inflation expectations.
The derived interest rate rule approximates the way the Bundesbank conducted monetary policy over the period 1975-1998.
The Bundesbank's policy reaction function showed strong persistence of policy rates.
The Bundesbank's policy reaction function responded strongly to deviations of inflation from target and to the activity growth gap.
The response of the Bundesbank's policy to the level of the output gap was not significant.
The paper compares the Bundesbank's monetary policy rule with those of the FED and the Bank of England.
The empirical analysis uses real-time data, as available to policy-makers at the time.
